text: Lessons six and seven introduced two specific security contexts — data access sets and business units — one at a time. This lesson pulls back and gives you the general concept, plus the fuller list Financials uses.

A security context is the specific element of the enterprise structure that a data security grant is scoped by — it answers "access to which dimension am I granting here." Oracle Fusion always requires a three way link: user, role, and data. The security context is what names the data side of that link precisely enough to enforce it.

In Financials, the contexts you'll see most are Business Unit, for Payables and Receivables; Data Access Set, for General Ledger; Ledger itself, in some assignment flows; Asset Book, for Fixed Assets; and Control Budget, for budgetary control. Each exists because it's the natural unit that module organizes its data around.

A complete role assignment is really four things bound together: the user, the role that defines what they can do, the security context naming the dimension, and the context value — the specific instance of that dimension. Change any one of those four and you have a different assignment. At Castellan Robotics, a new accountant named James Okafor gets role General Ledger Accountant, context Data Access Set, value East Division Data Access Set. Miss that context value, and James has the right job role but no actual ledger data to work with.

Security context names the dimension; context value names the specific instance. Together with user and role, that's the full anatomy of an assignment. Up next, lesson nine: provisioning users and roles, where you'll see how these assignments actually get created.
